facts.fact: Seriously Fish uses the name "bogwood" for this material.
bogwood: non-petrified wood that has been preserved in a peat bog, often used as aquarium decoration.
Vietnamese shops use the name "lũa thủy sinh" for aquarium driftwood.
Vietnamese shops also use the name "gỗ lũa" for aquarium driftwood.
An English-language magazine uses the name "driftwood" for wood used in aquariums.
Aquarium Care describes gỗ lũa as wood used to give an aquarium a natural habitat, and says its hard core resists termites.
TFH Magazine says all wood releases tannins, which can stain the water yellowish or tea-brown.
TFH Magazine says dense pieces of wood release tannins for longer than light, slender ones.
AquaSetup says tannins from lũa turn the water yellow or brown and lower pH slightly, but are not toxic to fish.
Cá Bảy Màu says tannin from lũa turns the water reddish-brown like tea, and can change pH and hardness, which can stress fish.
Gensou says tannins from wood may lower pH by about 0.2 to 0.5 in soft water, and less in well-buffered tap water.
TFH Magazine says the fuzz that grows on new wood comes from bacteria and fungi breaking down organic matter on the surface, and is generally harmless and fades over time.
AquaSetup says a white film may appear on lũa a few days after it goes into the tank. It is common and harmless, and usually goes away as the tank stabilises.
TFH Magazine says rinsing the wood in very hot water and scrubbing it with a brush helps remove fuzz.
Thái Hoà Aquarium says white mould on lũa can be scrubbed off with a brush, or left alone, since it often disappears by itself.
AquaSetup says shrimp, apple snails, pencilfish, otocinclus or plecos will eat the white film on lũa.
TFH Magazine says soaking, water changes, or activated carbon or other chemical filtration reduce tannin staining.
Gensou says tannins can be removed with activated carbon (replaced every two to four weeks), Purigen, or regular water changes.
Cá Bảy Màu advises changing 20–30% of the water daily for the first days after the lũa goes into the tank.
Thái Hoà Aquarium's steps: boil the wood first to clean it, kill algae and bacteria, and open its pores so it sinks.
Thái Hoà Aquarium: for pieces too large for a pot, pour hot water over the wood one section at a time.
Thái Hoà Aquarium: wood can be baked at no more than 121°C.
Thái Hoà Aquarium: one option is to scrub the wood, soak it in a 10% bleach solution, then rinse it with clean water.
Thái Hoà Aquarium: soak the wood in salt water for 1 week, then in plain water for 2 to 3 weeks.
Cá Bảy Màu: boil the lũa for about 30 minutes to 2 hours per round, changing the water each round until it stays clear.
Cá Bảy Màu: soak the lũa in plain water for 1 week to several months, changing the water daily or every 2–3 days.
Cá Bảy Màu: for large pieces, pour water at about 80–90°C over the wood section by section.
Cá Bảy Màu: soak in about 10% brine for about 1 week, rinse, then soak in clean water for 2–3 weeks.
AquaSetup: sun-dry wood you collect yourself for about 2 months or longer before using it.
AquaSetup: knock off loose soil, scrub with a dry brush, and sand off any bark left on with fine sandpaper.
AquaSetup: soak the wood for a few days to a week or two, which releases tannins and helps it sink.
Aquarium Care says dense, heavy wood does not need boiling: soaking it for a few days is enough for it to sink.
TFH Magazine advises rinsing wood in hot water and scrubbing it before soaking.
Thái Hoà Aquarium says dry lũa floats until it soaks up water, so it may need weights such as stones, or screws and silicone.
Cá Bảy Màu suggests weighting floating lũa with stones or lead, or holding it with suction cups.
AquaSetup says never to put fresh, unseasoned wood in the tank, and warns against pine in particular.
AquaSetup advises against boiling lũa, saying it can break down the wood's inner structure and make it rot faster.
AquaSetup warns that sharp or pointed pieces can tear the fins of long-finned fish such as bettas.
AquaSetup warns against pieces too large for the tank, which take away swimming space and make cleaning the substrate harder.
TFH Magazine says shoreline driftwood is salty and floats, so it is unsuitable for freshwater tanks.
TFH Magazine says conifers produce a lot of sap and some bark contains compounds that can harm fish, so research any unknown wood before using it.
TFH Magazine says wood that decomposes quickly can trigger bacterial blooms, algae and fungus. It singles out grapevine, which breaks down fast when wet.
Gensou advises using a dedicated pot to boil wood, because tannins stain the pot permanently.
Cá Bảy Màu advises against baking wood at home, and against using chemicals without rinsing thoroughly afterwards.
Cá Bảy Màu says wood that smells foul, has an unusual colour or sounds hollow when tapped may be rotten inside.
Gensou says Anubias, Bucephalandra and Java fern rhizomes tied to wood should not be buried, or they will rot.
Thái Hoà Aquarium warns that dead stumps of sú, vẹt and đước (mangrove trees) sold at the roadside in Vietnam are not durable and decay quickly.
Thái Hoà Aquarium warns that some smooth pieces of lũa with hollow 'eyes' are carved by hand and can be mistaken for natural wood.
Vietnamese shops sell lũa by the kilogram. Aqua Mart lists Lũa đỗ quyên at 200.000đ/kg.
Zen Aquarius sells driftwood under these names: Lũa kim sa tùng, Lũa hải sơn quỳ, Lũa xương chùm, Lũa rễ rừng, Lũa đỗ quyên việt, Lũa san đá ống, Lũa san đá miếng, Lũa san đá cành, Lũa thạch sùng.
Lũa sa tùng: Aquarium Care names "Lũa sa tùng" as one of six woods for planted tanks, and says it looks like a tall, ancient tree.
Lũa sa tùng: Thái Hoà Aquarium lists "Lũa Sa Tùng" among the driftwood types it sells.
Lũa sa tùng: Aquarium Care gives the same wood as both "gỗ lũa sa tùng" and "Lũa Kim Sa Tùng".
Lũa Kim sa tùng: Bống Vàng sells it as "Lũa Kim sa tùng 1kg", Aqua Mart as "Lũa kim sa tùng" and Zen Aquarius as "Lũa kim sa tùng (1kg)".
Lũa sa tùng: Brothers Concept sells it as "LŨA SA TÙNG CỔ THỤ NHÁNH".
Lũa sa tùng: no English trade name was found for this wood in any English-language shop or keeper source.
Lũa Kim sa tùng: Bống Vàng says its shape looks like an old tree standing tall, and that it is fully natural, with no pieces cut, joined or reworked.
Lũa kim sa tùng: Aqua Mart says it is made from carefully chosen branched sa tùng wood and is used for tying moss and for bonsai-style layouts.
Lũa Kim sa tùng: Bống Vàng says sa tùng wood does not leach colour into the water.
Lũa kim sa tùng: Zen Aquarius says the wood is boiled until cooked and its bark is scraped off clean before it is sold.
Lũa rễ rừng: Aqua Mart sells "Lũa rễ rừng" at a page whose web address reads lua-sa-tung. It is driftwood made from roots, sold stripped of bark, cleaned and dried.
Lũa đỗ quyên: Aqua Mart sells it as "Lũa đỗ quyên", Thủy Sinh Tím as "Lũa Đỗ Quyên HN 1kg" and Zen Aquarius as "Lũa đỗ quyên việt (1kg)".
Lũa đỗ quyên: English-language shops sell the same azalea or rhododendron root as "spider wood". Gensou also calls it "azalea root" or "rhododendron root".
Spider Wood: BRS also lists it as "Spider Wood / Cuckoo Root".
Lũa Đỗ Quyên HN 1kg: Thủy Sinh Tím describes a root system with many twisted branches, yellow-brown, with thick trunk sections.
Lũa đỗ quyên: Aqua Mart says it is usually used as one whole natural piece, not joined from smaller pieces, and suits a somewhat larger tank.
Lũa đỗ quyên việt: Zen Aquarius says most pieces are sold unpeeled and are used in BioTop-style tanks that are mostly wood with few plants, with fish such as discus or angelfish.
Spider wood: Gensou says it is light and floats at first. Thin branches waterlog in one to two weeks, and the thicker centre can take two to six weeks.
Red spider wood: TFH Magazine says it floats at first and can take up to a month to sink.
Spider wood: Gensou says it releases tannins that tint the water yellow to amber-brown.
Spider wood: Gensou says a white, fuzzy film often appears in the first one to four weeks. It is a bacterial film, not a fungal infection, is harmless, and shrimp, snails and Otocinclus eat it.
Spider wood: Gensou advises soaking it for one to two weeks with a water change every two to three days, boiling it in a dedicated pot, and scrubbing off loose bark.
Spider wood: TFH Magazine advises soaking it two to four weeks with weekly hot-water changes and a weight to keep it under, or screwing it to a slate base so it sinks at once.
Spider wood: Gensou says boiling it for one to two hours speeds sinking but can soften thin branches and break fragile tips.
Lũa Cholla: Thủy Sinh Tím sells cholla as "Lũa Cholla Bé", "Lũa Cholla Trung", "Lũa Cholla Lớn" and "Lũa Cholla Đại". BRS sells it in English as "Cholla Wood".
Lũa Cholla Bé: Thủy Sinh Tím says it is the dead stem of the Staghorn Cholla cactus (Cylindropuntia) from North American deserts, brown to red, full of holes and grooves.
Lũa Cholla Bé: Thủy Sinh Tím says it floats at first and sinks by itself after about 1–2 days in the tank.
Lũa Cholla Bé: Thủy Sinh Tím says it releases tannins, gives shrimp shelter during breeding and moulting, and grows biofilm that baby shrimp eat.
Lũa Cholla Bé: Thủy Sinh Tím advises simmering it on low heat for about 30 minutes before use, or soaking it for about 3–4 days.
Lũa Cholla Bé: Thủy Sinh Tím says the wood wears down noticeably after 6–8 months.
Cholla wood: Gensou says it is soft and slowly breaks down over about 6 to 12 months, so it is semi-disposable.
Mopani: VIETPET sells Zoo Med's mopani as "Gỗ lũa cho bể cá Zoo Med Mopani". Tannin Aquatics sells it in English as "Mopani".
Mopani: Tannin Aquatics says it comes from the tree Colophospermum mopane, which grows only in hot, dry parts of Africa.
Gỗ lũa cho bể cá Zoo Med Mopani: VIETPET says it sinks right away and has a smooth, mottled surface.
African root wood (Mopani): TFH Magazine says it is tan outside and dark mahogany inside, dense, sinks quickly and often forms caves.
Mopani: Tannin Aquatics says it keeps leaching tannins that tint the water for a long time. TFH Magazine says African root wood releases a lot of tannins over a long period.
Mopani: Tannin Aquatics advises rinsing it, scrubbing it lightly with a soft brush, and soaking it in fresh water for one to two weeks. Small pieces can be boiled and then soaked for a few days.
African root wood: TFH Magazine advises soaking it one to three weeks, and says boiling speeds tannin removal.
Mopani: Tannin Aquatics says plecos and other catfish may gnaw on it, though they prefer softer wood.
Malaysian Driftwood: BRS sells it in English as "Malaysian Driftwood". No Vietnamese shop page found sells it under a Vietnamese name.
Malaysian driftwood: Gensou says it is mangrove root wood that sinks almost at once, often within a day or two of soaking.
Malaysian driftwood: TFH Magazine says it is dark, dense, usually sinks, and is among the cheapest woods.
Malaysian driftwood: Gensou says it releases few tannins compared with lighter woods.
Malaysian wood: TFH Magazine advises soaking it about a week.
Manzanita: TFH Magazine and Gensou use the English name "Manzanita". No Vietnamese shop page found sells it under a Vietnamese name.
Manzanita: Gensou says it is dense, hard wood from a North American shrub, sinks more readily than spider wood and releases fewer tannins.
Manzanita: TFH Magazine describes it as pale, light and twiggy. It does not sink by itself, and its branches can be sharp enough to injure large or active fish.
Manzanita: TFH Magazine advises soaking it three to four weeks, weighted down.
Manzanita: Gensou says its smooth bark holds moss poorly.
Bogwood: no Vietnamese shop page found sells it under a Vietnamese name.
Lũa linh sam: Aquarium Care says "Gỗ lũa linh sam" is the most popular decorative wood and has natural wave-like grain.
Lũa trà gừng: Aquarium Care says "Lũa trà gừng" has many branches that are joined together into a layout.
Lũa hải sơn tùng: Aquarium Care says "Lũa hải sơn tùng" keeps its natural form and texture.
Lũa xương trùm: Aquarium Care says "Lũa xương trùm" can be shaped into tree canopies, caves or small hills.
Lũa nhọ nồi: Aqua Mart's own page sells driftwood under the name "Lũa nhọ nồi".
Lũa hải sơn quỳ: Zen Aquarius's own page sells driftwood under the name "Lũa hải sơn quỳ (1kg)".
Lũa san đá: Zen Aquarius's own page sells driftwood under the names "Lũa san đá ống (1kg)", "Lũa san đá miếng (1kg)" and "Lũa san đá cành (1kg)".
Lũa thạch sùng: Zen Aquarius's own page sells driftwood under the name "Lũa thạch sùng (1kg)".
AquaSetup says đào and đỗ quyên have toxic leaves, but their wood has little or no toxicity.
Gensou says the white film on new spider wood is a bacterial film, not a fungal infection.
Name for the term: "bogwood".
Name for the term: "driftwood".
Name for the term: "lũa thủy sinh".
Name for the term: "gỗ lũa thủy sinh".
Bogwood is wood that is not petrified and has been preserved in a peat bog. It is often used to decorate aquaria.
Tannins leach out of driftwood and tint the water. They do not harm fish but slowly lower pH a little.
A tea-coloured tank looks like the Amazon blackwater habitats where tetras live.
Wood is mostly cellulose and does not lower pH in any meaningful way. Tannic acid lowers it only slightly, and water hardness buffers the change.
Once the bark is off, wood cannot make ammonia, nitrite or nitrate as it decays, because cellulose contains no nitrogen.
The author estimates that wood releases nitrogen at parts per billion per day, which is too little to cause a spike.
In a Walstad-style planted tank, wood can reduce the nitrogen available, because the fungi and molds living on it use nitrogen up.
The author's wood usually lasts about three years, but there is no reliable way to predict how long a piece will last.
Whether a wood is hard or soft does not predict how long it lasts. Its tannin content and how long it has been dead matter more.
Tannin is not harmful to fish, but the colour may look unattractive. It suits biotope-style tanks.
Low tannin levels turn water pale yellow and high levels turn it deep yellow.
Tannin can turn water yellowish, tea-coloured or brown. High tannin can make the pH drop sharply.
Lũa is hard, is not damaged by termites or borers, and does not rot under water.
White film on new wood is usually a bacterial biofilm, not a true fungus. It feeds on sugars, tannins and cellulose leaching from the wood.
The white biofilm is harmless to fish, shrimp, snails and plants.
The white film first appears on days 2–5, starting in crevices and rough areas.
The white film peaks in weeks 1–2, when it spreads across more of the wood.
The white film starts to shrink in weeks 2–3 and is gone by weeks 3–6. It can come back in waves, each usually weaker. Warm water speeds up both its growth and its clearing.
A white film is common on new wood. It usually lasts four to five weeks and may smell slightly.
New lũa often grows a white film (nhớt trắng) early on. It usually fades if the tank is stable, there are suitable cleaning animals and water is changed regularly.
Do not confuse the biofilm on wood with cottony white growth on fish, which may be a fungal infection (Saprolegnia) that needs treatment.
A foul smell, or growth that lasts beyond 8 weeks, may mean the wood is rotting.
Remove the wood if the film persists, the smell worsens or the wood starts to fall apart. This happens more often with wood collected from woods than from water.

Animals that graze the white biofilm include Neocaridina shrimp (cherry shrimp and colour variants), Amano shrimp, nerite snails, mystery snails, Malaysian trumpet snails, Otocinclus and bristlenose plecos.
Shrimp, snails and Otocinclus graze the white film on spider wood. The film fades once the easily digested organics are used up.
Activated carbon or Purigen removes tannins. Replace the media when it stops working, which can take from two weeks to two months.
Purigen or activated carbon can clear tannin colour from wood that keeps leaching after curing.
Plan the layout on paper before placing the wood, because rearranging later can stress the tank.
Scrub the wood well with a clean brush, without soap or chemical cleaners.

Cure the wood fully submerged in a large bucket for at least 1 to 2 weeks. Drain and rinse whenever the water darkens, and refill with dechlorinated or RO water until the water stays clear for several days in a row.
Boil the wood for 1 to 2 hours in a large stockpot. This speeds tannin release and kills algal or fungal spores.
Anchor large floating pieces to rocks with monofilament fishing line.
Clean lũa by scrubbing with a brush or a pressure hose to remove leftover bark and mud.
Soak lũa for 2–4 weeks depending on the type, changing the water periodically. Large pieces can soak in a big container or in a new tank with no fish.
Boil small pieces of lũa for 1–2 hours. Industrial alcohol or hydrogen peroxide can speed up the process. Afterwards rinse or re-soak the wood, then dry it in the sun.
Soak lũa without bark for about 1 week, then dry it in the sun to make leftover bark easier to peel.
Boil small pieces of lũa in hot water for about 3–4 hours each time to sterilise them.
For deeper cleaning of large pieces, soak them in water with industrial hydrogen peroxide and sulfur.
First scrub off dust, soil, dried algae and any soft, rotten or smelly wood with a stiff brush. Then boil the piece, or pour hot water over large pieces several times, or boil them in sections.
After boiling, soak lũa in clean water, changing it regularly. Before adding it to the tank, check that it is clean, firm and sinks, and that it no longer leaches colour.
Soaking lũa takes about 1 to 6 months and removes resin, toxins and colour.
Boiling can cut the preparation time by about 50% to 70%, but it only suits small or loose pieces, not large solid ones.
Hydrogen peroxide ("OXY già") or industrial alcohol can cut the preparation time by about 40% to 50%.
To prevent white biofilm: boil the wood for 1–2 hours, or soak it for 1–4 weeks with water changes every few days if it is too big to boil, and scrub it with a stiff brush under hot running water.
Wood can be cured for 24 hours in about 1 part 3% hydrogen peroxide to 3 parts water, then rinsed well.
Smell wood before use. A chemical or turpentine smell means do not use it. Drill into sappy areas: sappy shavings mean the wood needs more weathering.
Boiling does not make wood sink and can make it softer and quicker to decay. Wood sinks after long submersion, so weigh it down with rocks or ornaments meanwhile.
If wood needs sterilising, hydrogen peroxide or potassium permanganate is safer than bleach. Soaking stream wood in either may help against hydra or planaria in shrimp tanks.
Weathered, odour-free wood usually needs only weighting down and patience. It does not need to be cleaned, sealed or baked.
Buying driftwood sold for reptiles is a mistake, because it may contain chemicals harmful to fish.
Wood or roots collected outdoors are often not properly dried or cured and can rot in the tank.
Soap or chemical cleaners leave residue that will poison the aquarium.
Remove the monofilament line from Java moss or Java fern once they have grown onto the wood.
Never use bleach on wood. Sodium hypochlorite can stay in the wood, and water conditioners may not neutralise it.
Some suppliers oil their wood, and the author says this has killed fish. Wood used in reptile tanks or treated for looks may also release nitrogen compounds.
Wood that was dried and then wetted again can release ammonia from the organisms that died on it.
Adding wood at the same time as a water change can hide the real cause of any problem that follows.
Avoid fresh pine or cedar and wood with a strong sap or eucalyptus smell. Fresh pine and cedar can be toxic to fish, but weathered wood that no longer smells is considered harmless.
Common mistakes include adding lũa after only a quick rinse, adding it while it still leaches colour or smells, keeping soft rotting wood, and weighing it down with unsuitable materials.
Treating yellow water with harsh methods can destabilise the tank.
The shop advises against the product "Thủy Sinh 4U" for treating lũa because of possible side effects. It also warns that torching lũa can discolour or damage it.
Buying lũa before deciding on the layout is a mistake, because each type suits different designs.
Do not remove harmless biofilm by taking the wood out.
Boil spider wood in a pot kept only for this, not a cooking pot. Use only stainless steel screws, because other metals corrode.
For slime and colour released by new lũa, add cleaner animals such as red cherry shrimp, or change the water regularly for a while.
Floating new lũa is normal. Soak it longer or anchor it to a heavy base such as stones.
Weigh floating lũa down with wood or stone until it sinks.
Myth: boiling wood kills pathogens and removes tannins. Aquariumscience.org says boiling removes tannins only from the outer layer, and deeper tannins can leach for months or years.
Myth: decaying wood causes ammonia spikes. Aquariumscience.org says this is chemically impossible and blames reported spikes on coincident water changes, chlorine pulses or poor oxygenation.
Myth: tannins have antibacterial or antifungal benefits. Aquariumscience.org says tannins would need about 2,000 ppm, which makes water nearly opaque.
Myth: you should sterilise wood with bleach. Aquariumscience.org calls this the most dangerous myth.
Aquariumscience.org also rejects these myths: only hardwoods are suitable, ocean driftwood has enough salt to harm fish, and wood is often contaminated with pesticides.
Myth: baking wood is useful. Aquariumscience.org says it does nothing useful and is a fire risk.
Lũa đỗ quyên: wood with many branches. The branches are soft and curved, more yellow than other woods, and easy to arrange and attach plants to.
Lũa đỗ quyên: darkens to a deep brown as it soaks up water.
Lũa đỗ quyên: yellow when new, it turns brown after soaking for a while. Early on it tends to release an oily film.
Lũa đỗ quyên: usually sinks after about 1 day to several weeks, depending on the size of the piece. It has attractive, glossy grain.
Lũa đỗ quyên (incl. Lũa đỗ quyên việt and Lũa đỗ quyên xoắn): solid single pieces that need little joining. The twisted type (xoắn) comes from fresh wood with soft, twisting roots.
Lũa đỗ quyên: sold as wood from the đỗ quyên tree.
Lũa Đỗ Quyên HN 1kg: yellow-brown with a solid yellow core in the base and roots. It has thick trunk sections and several curved branches that can be arranged into bonsai-like shapes.
Lũa Đỗ Quyên HN 1kg: sold by the kilogram at 240.000₫.
Spider wood: also called azalea root or rhododendron root, from the root systems of azalea and rhododendron shrubs. It has thin, tangled, web-like branches.
Spider wood: golden to reddish brown when dry, it darkens to a warm brown under water.
Spider wood: light and floats for a long time. Thin branches may waterlog within a week or two, while the thick centre can take two to six weeks or more.
Spider wood: to keep it down, screw it to a stone with stainless steel, glue it to rock with cyanoacrylate gel, wedge it between rocks, or wait for it to waterlog.
Spider wood: tints water yellow to amber-brown. Its tannins may lower pH by about 0.2–0.5 in soft water.
Spider wood: soak it weighted under water for 1–2 weeks, changing the water every 2–3 days, or boil small pieces for 1–2 hours.
Spider wood: a white, fuzzy biofilm often appears in the first 1–4 weeks.
Spider wood (azalea root): releases a lot of tannin when first submerged and often needs weighing down for 1–3 weeks until it waterlogs. It suits forest canopy and bonsai-style layouts.
Spiderwood (also called azalea root): known for heavy biofilm.
Lũa linh sam: one of the most common woods for aquascape layouts. It comes in many sizes, with grain patterns on the surface and shapes from straight to curved.
Lũa linh sam: sinks easily but releases colour into the water, so water needs frequent changes early on.
Lũa linh sam: sinks almost straight away but releases yellow colour into the water for a long time.
Lũa linh sam: brown, twisted and irregular. The shop says it sinks without stones, does not release colour ("Không ra màu") and is non-toxic to fish.
Lũa Sa Tùng: listed by Thái Hoà Aquarium among the lũa types it sells for aquascapes.
Lũa Kim sa tùng 1kg: made from "gỗ sa tùng", shaped like an old tree standing upright, and natural rather than cut and joined. The shop says it does not leach colour. Price 220.000 ₫.
Lũa kim sa tùng: described as "gỗ sa tùng nhánh" (branch-type sa tùng wood). Sold for aquarium and paludarium aquascapes, for tying moss and making bonsai-style pieces.
Lũa kim sa tùng (1kg): sa tùng wood boiled until cooked, with the bark scraped off before sale. The shop says it does not release colour. Price 120.000 ₫.
LŨA SA TÙNG CỔ THỤ GỐC: base wood from an old sa tùng tree, boiled and scraped clean of bark. The shop says sa tùng wood does not leach colour into the water.
Lũa sa tùng: none of the pages read names the botanical tree. Shops sell it only as "gỗ sa tùng" (sa tùng wood) shaped like an ancient tree.
Lũa hải sơn quỳ (also called lũa hải sa): sinks naturally, turns water cloudy white rather than yellow-red, needs little preparation, and comes in varied, compact shapes.

Lũa hải sơn quỳ: sold as a whole trunk with its roots. The trunk is mostly straight with a slight curve, with a small set of root branches below. It needs little cutting and can stand as a vertical pillar in a layout.
Lũa Hải Sơn Quỳ: a root base with many small branches, coloured yellow and reddish-brown. Listed as sinking 100%, releasing no colour, with the bark removed, ready for the tank.
Lũa Hải sa quỳ: close to a complete root with branches, with the bark removed. The shop says it releases no colour or odour and can go straight into the tank. Price 132.000 ₫.
Lũa long vân quỳ: also called "Lũa hải sơn quỳ" on this page. It has many roots and small branches and is popular for bonsai layouts.
Lũa trà rừng: sinks readily and does not lose colour in water. Hobbyists in southern Vietnam often use it.
Lũa trà rừng: the shop says it sinks as soon as it is put in the tank and does not discolour the water. The pieces can be joined into different shapes.
Lũa bonsai / lũa xương chùm: root and trunk pieces shaped like bonsai trees, with relatively high tannin. Mosses, bucep or ráy can be attached to it.
Lũa bonsai / lũa xương chùm: sharp edges can injure long-finned fish such as betta and guppies. It costs more than other types.
Lũa cây bon sai: the name under which Nhật Đình lists bonsai driftwood.
Lũa xương chùm: small, canopy-shaped pieces, often used as the canopy for bonsai-style lũa.
Lũa xương chùm: light and does not sink, so it is joined to heavier wood such as Lũa Linh Sam or tied to a stone. The shop says it releases no colour, and 1 kg makes two or three bonsai pieces.
Lũa Xương Chùm 1kg: bone-like, interlocking branch clusters, attached to larger branches as bonsai canopies and covered with moss. Price 300,000₫.
Lũa rễ rừng: small, long, soft roots that grow in clusters. Used as root structure for bonsai wood and for block-type roots like hải sơn quỳ, and popular in blackwater biotope tanks.
Lũa thạch sùng: straight wood that has been processed but keeps its bark, for a more natural look. It is often paired with lũa rễ rừng to look like large forest trees.
Lũa thạch sùng thẳng 1kg: firm, sturdy driftwood with attractive grain, from mountain forests in central Vietnam. Used for old-growth forest ("rừng cổ thụ") layouts. Price 110.000 ₫.
Lũa Thạch Sùng (1kg): from forests in central Vietnam, for forest-style layouts. Price 70,000₫.
Lũa rễ 1kg: root-shaped, like a ginseng root. Sold either peeled, cleaned and dried, or unpeeled, for root structures, bonsai and forest layouts.
Lũa săn đá: made from a large trunk that eroded over time, leaving only part of it. It is a hollow, medium-to-large block with many grain streaks and can go into a layout without cutting.
Lũa săn đá: from mountain forests in central Vietnam, weathered by rain, sun and wind down to a hard core with twisting grain. Sold at 110,000 ₫ per 1 kg.
Lũa San Đá Miếng (1kg): wind and sun leave only the hard, dense core ("săn đá") of a large trunk. It is irregular with twisting grain.
Lũa San Đá Miếng (1kg): early on it releases some white slime and may turn the water yellow. Soak it 3–5 days and rinse, or boil it for 10 minutes. Purigen can remove the yellow tint.
Lũa san đá: Zen Aquarius sells it as "lũa san đá ống, san đá miếng, san đá cành", alongside lũa hải sơn quỳ and lũa xương chùm.
Lũa vân thép – san đá: worn by rain, sun and wind down to the core, with irregular shapes and winding grain.
Lũa thép (vân thép): a newer, rough, very hard wood similar to linh sam. Its grain lines stand out under water, and it is used in nano and shallow tanks.
Lũa nhọ nồi: many branches that droop or spread. It suits simple biotope layouts and beginners.

Lũa nhọ nồi (1kg): from forests in central Vietnam, with many small, irregular branches. Used for wall mounting, biotopes and attaching plants. The bark must be removed and the wood cleaned before use. Price 275.000 ₫.
Lũa sừng: yellow rather than brown-yellow, with curves like leaf veins or irregular waves. Large pieces are often used in discus and angelfish tanks and rainforest paludariums.
Hải Sơn Tùng and Ngọc Linh Sam: dry woods that are sometimes used as lũa.
Lũa Hải Sơn Tùng: listed by Thái Hoà Aquarium among its lũa types, along with Lũa Nguyệt Quế, Lũa Dã Quỳ and Lũa nhẹ Hải Ninh.
Lũa cholla: dried wood of a cactus from the deserts of Arizona and New Mexico. It is a hollow cylinder with many small holes, popular in shrimp tanks and as hiding spots for young fish.
Lũa Cholla Bé: made from the trunk of the Staghorn Cholla cactus (Cylindropuntia) after it dies naturally. Brown to red, with holes and grooves.
Lũa Cholla Bé: floats at first and sinks by itself after about 1–2 days. Boil it on low heat for about 30 minutes before use, or soak it, which takes about 3–4 days longer.
Lũa Cholla Bé: the shop says it releases tannins, acidifies and softens the water, lowers pH, and gives shrimp hiding places and biofilm to graze.
Cholla wood: very light and must be soaked to sink. It is soft and slowly decomposes over 6–12 months, which the source calls a "semi-disposable hardscape element".
Cholla wood: popular in shrimp tanks, with moderate biofilm.
Malaysian driftwood (mangrove root): dark brown to nearly black, dense and heavy. It sinks almost at once, often within a day or two, releases little tannin and needs little preparation.
Malaysian driftwood: dense and hard, so it usually grows less biofilm.
Manzanita: wood from a North American shrub. It is dense and hard with smooth bark and reddish-brown tones, sinks more readily than spider wood, and releases fewer tannins.
Manzanita: its smooth surface holds moss poorly, and it is less prone to biofilm than spider wood.
Mopani: the heartwood of Colophospermum mopane, a legume tree from southern Africa. Its density of 1.2 to 1.4 g/cm³ makes it sink at once.
Mopani: releases heavy tannins for 8 to 12 weeks, with leaching near zero after about six months. It lowers pH 6.8–7.2 water to roughly 6.2–6.6 in the first month.
Mopani: suits Apistogramma, tetras, wild Betta and shrimp, but not Mbuna or other hard-water cichlids.

Mopani: soak it with water changes every 48 hours. A 3-week soak removes about half the tannins and 4 weeks about 70%. Or boil small pieces for 60 to 90 minutes, repeat in fresh water, then cold-soak for 7 days.
Mopani: a white haze may appear in weeks 2 to 4 and usually clears by week 6.
Mopani wood: dense and hard, so it usually grows less biofilm.
Bống Vàng sells lũa nhọ nồi, săn đá, thạch sùng and rễ as wood harvested from forests in central Vietnam.
Vietnamese shops sell lũa by the kilogram. For example, Lũa săn đá costs 110,000 ₫ and Lũa San Đá Miếng costs 70,000₫ per 1 kg.
Thủy Sinh Tím sells cholla under the names "Lũa Cholla Bé", "Lũa Cholla Trung", "Lũa Cholla Lớn" and "Lũa Cholla Đại".
